item.title: Linux Mint replaced Ubuntu as the best first distro, and Ubuntu's own choices explain why
item.itunes:title: Linux Mint replaced Ubuntu as the best first distro, and Ubuntu's own choices explain why
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you went a decade back in time and asked someone in the Linux community what the best beginner distro was, there's a good chance they'd reply with Ubuntu. It's what I heard a lot about when I first dipped my toe into the world of FOSS operating systems, and for good reason.

Fast forward to today, and that has changed. Ubuntu isn't the beginner's dream anymore; not because it's bad, but because the world of Linux has evolved to make it easier than ever to get started.

Ubuntu used to be a beginner's ideal first distro...

It lowered the bar for a lot of adopters

When I first used Ubuntu around 2010, I remember that one of its biggest draws was that it installed like a regular operating system. At the time, using Linux was pretty obtuse, and it was great to have something I could install similarly to Windows. There were even Ubuntu install disks you could pop into your CD tray and run.

Ubuntu was surprisingly easy to run. It recognised most of my hardware right off the bat, looked somewhat similar to Windows, and even came with an incredible boot-up sound that I found endearing. And that was a huge part of Ubuntu. In fact, that's why it's called Ubuntu; the name is based on a Nguni Bantu philosophy meaning "humanity towards others."

And that's why it was the default recommendation at the time. It was made for people and was approachable for someone like me, who didn't want to have their head stuck in the guts of an operating system just to have something workable.

Unfortunately, gaming support at the time was pretty abysmal, so I'd float back to Windows and wouldn't touch Linux again for another 15 years.

I used lightweight Linux to revive a Windows PC that Microsoft gave up on, and it's not Ubuntu

An aging 2012 laptop shed its bloat and booted in minutes with a stripped Fluxbox setup that sips under 500MB of RAM.

4
By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

...but it had lost that title when I came back to Linux

The bar had somehow gotten even lower for newcomers

When I wanted to give Linux a second stab in the middle of 2025 to give my aging Windows 10 PC a longer life before end-of-support, I did some research into which OS would be good for a beginner. I still had Ubuntu in the back of my mind, but when I did research on what OS would be best for me, I found that Linux Mint was the one everyone recommended for a Windows user. So, I gave Linux Mint a try, and now, almost a year and a half later, I'm still on Linux. Not on Linux Mint (it's openSUSE Tumbleweed right now), but very much a big fan of Team Tux.

Linux Mint hit on all the things that got me interested in Ubuntu 15 years ago, and then some. It was simple to install, worked out of the box, and treated me like a human being. However, it also had much better support for the apps I enjoyed on Windows, such as Chrome and Steam. On top of that, it had a very similar look and feel to Windows, meaning I felt right at home from day one.

Linux Mint isn't the answer for Windows refugees anymore

It's still good, but not the best.

147
By  Simon Batt

Ubuntu just doesn't have the beginner-attracting power anymore

I really dislike how it evolved over the years

Eventually, Linux Mint would become too small for my ambitions. I didn't want "Linux but Windows-flavored" anymore; I wanted an OS that challenged me with something new to explore. So, I went distro-hopping, and part of my tour landed me on my old favorite, Ubuntu.

I don't think I rebounded off Ubuntu harder than any OS I tried during that session. The reason was GNOME, something I would quickly learn was very much not for me. As soon as I logged on, everything felt alien; bars were placed where I didn't like them being placed, buttons didn't do what I thought they did, and I felt like I was fighting the desktop environment more than I was using it.

Eventually, I would discover that KDE was my desktop environment of choice. And, yes, there is Kubuntu, which is Ubuntu with all the KDE trimmings; however, by the time I had even learned what distro flavors were, I had already fallen in love with Fedora KDE and Flatpaks. And after learning that Ubuntu was more of a fan of Snaps, I never went back.

Canonical is speeding up Ubuntu's kernel updates because it's drowning in AI-discovered bugs

AI bug hunting is the new normal.

2
By  Simon Batt

Ubuntu is fine, but there are better options now

While Ubuntu was the ideal beginner OS back in the early 2010s, I would second-guess recommending it to a newcomer today. I think Linux Mint does a far better job of getting people introduced to the world of FOSS, although that doesn't mean people can't discover it for themselves later.

item.title: I gave my local LLM a nearly-full SSD and told it to find everything I could safely delete
item.itunes:title: I gave my local LLM a nearly-full SSD and told it to find everything I could safely delete
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Every couple of weeks, my 1TB SSD starts to fill to the brim for one reason or another. And every time, the fix is to open WizTree, go through the biggest files and folders one after another, and decide what can go. WizTree is excellent at showing me where the space went, but it won't tell me which of those files are safe to remove, and that's something that takes up a huge chunk of my time.

I started to wonder whether an open-weights model could undertake that review for me, with nothing to go on but my WizTree export. So I gave Qwen3.6 a map of my drive and asked what I could safely delete. It didn't have a way to undertake any actions itself, but it could look around and report back with whatever I could lose on my drive. Here's how it went.

The model could see every file, but touch none

Read-only access, a single system prompt, with zero hand-holding

The specific model I ran was Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at UD-IQ4_XS quant on llama.cpp, with a 32K token context. This is an open-weights, Mixture-of-Experts model with 35B total parameters and 3B active, released under the Apache 2.0 license, and it ran on my RTX 4070 Ti Super with 16GB of GDDR6X memory, with some of its expert layers offloaded to system RAM. I used the sampler settings from the model card.

Setting

Value

Model

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (UD-IQ4_XS)

Runtime

llama.cpp

Context

32,768 tokens

Sampling

Temperature 1.0, top-k 20, top-p 0.95

As stated before, the model never touched my drive directly. I exported a full scan from WizTree and loaded it into a small SQLite database. The model itself got four lookups, including the largest files, folder sizes, the files inside a folder, and totals by file type. To keep the conversation inside the context window, the model only saw its most recent lookups, and older results dropped out of the view as it went. I also decided to keep my Downloads folder and some personal app data out of the database for privacy.

The model's only tools were those four read-only lookups, each capped at 60 rows per call. It had no web search, no code execution and no way to otherwise open files. A python script talked to llama.cpp directly, with no chat interface in between. The model's thinking mode was on, but reasoning from earlier turns wasn't sent back to it, and each reply was capped at 8,192 tokens, which none of its responses reached.

The system prompt was short and as straightforward as it could get:

"You are auditing a nearly-full Windows 11 system drive. You have read-only access, through the provided functions, to a database of every file and folder on it. You cannot delete anything. Find what can be safely deleted to free up space and report it. For each item, give its path, its size, and why it is safe to remove. Never propose user documents, photos, or personal files. If you are not sure something is safe to delete, say so rather than claiming it is."

It's worth noting here that this wasn't my first or only attempt. Earlier runs hit bugs in the script, including conversations that overflowed the context window and final answers that came back empty, with some using an earlier version of the database before I removed personal, identifiable data. The published findings come from one run, the first on the final database and the finished script, and it's the only generation I'm reporting here.

I finally found a local LLM I want to use every day (and it's not for coding)

Local AI that actually fits into my day

21
By  Nolen Jonker

It found 17GB of data safe to delete

But there's a "cache 22" situation

The model's report promised to free about 17GB of storage, and almost all of that came from one file, which was a 16GB rolling cache Microsoft Flight Simulator keeps in AppData. This was reasonable given the constraints, but the problem was that, the moment I launched the sim again, the program would create a new rolling cache when it starts.

The rest of the recommendations were more useful. It found about 500MB of Microsoft Edge caches and 150MB of files in the Temp folder, which isn't much, but both are absolutely safe to clear.

Funnily enough, the next recommendation was to delete C:\Program Files\llamacpp, describing it as a local AI toolkit I could remove if I wasn't running local models. I was running the model through llama.cpp at that exact moment. To be fair, that folder was a second installation, so I can understand why that had been tripping the model up. For a duplicate file, the model does earn a point. It was, however, concerning to see that the model didn't say that it was uncertain about this.

It also claimed that "installed games (Epic Games" was to blame for a big chunk of my storage, but my three biggest games on the drive are Red Dead Redemption 2, Star Wars Jedi: Survivor and Resident Evil Requiem, not one of which came from Epic.

I ditched cloud AI for these 3 local models, and my 8GB GPU handles them all

8GB may not be great for games, but it can be more than enough for these local models

1
By  Abhinav Raj

It snatched defeat from the jaws of victory

Looking isn't the same as reporting, apparently

The logs recorded every single lookup the model made, and that's where I caught the next problem. On its second turn, it opened the Recycle bin and listed everything inside, which was at that time holding 21GB of files I had already deleted. Emptying it was the safest path towards a cleanup, and yet, it was missing from the report.

A couple of turns later, it found a 7.4GB crash report in Windows' LiveKernelReports folder. Windows tends to write these whenever a driver becomes unresponsive, and they're generally safe to remove when not needed for further troubleshooting. This too, was listed by the model, but was left out of the report.

Turn 7 it checked Nvidia's DXCache folder and saw 6.5GB of shader cache. This is a folder that I've written about before, and removing it is safe considering Nvidia re-builds it as games require it. This was left out of the report as well.

These items did not make it to the final report, but in retrospect, a part of the limitation is the setup it ran on. The model file itself is 16.5GB and my RTX 4070 Ti Super has 16GB of memory, and so some of it already runs from system RAM. One might argue that a bigger context window might catch those early finds, and that is a fair assumption. At 32K, the model could only see its most recent lookups, so the Recycle Bin, crash report, and shader cache could have been dropped out of the view before the response.

A bigger window would push even more of the model off the GPU and slow everything down from the 65–70 tokens/second I was seeing, and that is a trade off most people running local models on a gaming card might run into.

496MB

Turns 8-10

Would I recommend doing this?

Perhaps the most honest answer that I can muster is that one run don't really provide enough to write a decisive verdict. That being said, I'm not comfortable handing disk cleanup to a local model yet. The feat that's worth writing home about is the fact that Qwen3.6 never made a recommendation that would harm the system, and the most grievous error here is just lost opportunity. It's a good approach if you're looking at the logs to get a hint at possible places that may warrant a clean-up, but for any other actions, the model wasn't quite there for me yet.

The model itself got four lookups, including the largest files, folder sizes, the files inside a folder, and totals by file type. To keep the conversation inside the context window, the model only saw its most recent lookups, and older results dropped out of the view as it went. I also decided to keep my Downloads folder and some personal app data out of the database for privacy.

The model's only tools were those four read-only lookups, each capped at 60 rows per call. It had no web search, no code execution and no way to otherwise open files. A python script talked to llama.cpp directly, with no chat interface in between. The model's thinking mode was on, but reasoning from earlier turns wasn't sent back to it, and each reply was capped at 8,192 tokens, which none of its responses reached.

The system prompt was short and as straightforward as it could get:

"You are auditing a nearly-full Windows 11 system drive. You have read-only access, through the provided functions, to a database of every file and folder on it. You cannot delete anything. Find what can be safely deleted to free up space and report it. For each item, give its path, its size, and why it is safe to remove. Never propose user documents, photos, or personal files. If you are not sure something is safe to delete, say so rather than claiming it is."

It's worth noting here that this wasn't my first or only attempt. Earlier runs hit bugs in the script, including conversations that overflowed the context window and final answers that came back empty, with some using an earlier version of the database before I removed personal, identifiable data. Local AI that actually fits into my day

It found 17GB of data safe to delete

But there's a "cache 22" situation

The model's report promised to free about 17GB of storage, and almost all of that came from one file, which was a 16GB rolling cache Microsoft Flight Simulator keeps in AppData. This was reasonable given the constraints, but the problem was that, the moment I launched the sim again, the program would create a new rolling cache when it starts.

The rest of the recommendations were more useful. It found about 500MB of Microsoft Edge caches and 150MB of files in the Temp folder, which isn't much, but both are absolutely safe to clear.

Funnily enough, the next recommendation was to delete C:\Program Files\llamacpp, describing it as a local AI toolkit I could remove if I wasn't running local models. I was running the model through llama.cpp at that exact moment. To be fair, that folder was a second installation, so I can understand why that had been tripping the model up. For a duplicate file, the model does earn a point. It was, however, concerning to see that the model didn't say that it was uncertain about this.

It also claimed that "installed games (Epic Games" was to blame for a big chunk of my storage, but my three biggest games on the drive are Red Dead Redemption 2, Star Wars Jedi: Survivor and Resident Evil Requiem, not one of which came from Epic.

8GB may not be great for games, but it can be more than enough for these local models

It snatched defeat from the jaws of victory

Looking isn't the same as reporting, apparently

Perhaps the most honest answer that I can muster is that one run don't really provide enough to write a decisive verdict. That being said, I'm not comfortable handing disk cleanup to a local model yet. item.title: 4 useful Jellyfin apps that make my self-hosted server so much better
item.itunes:title: 4 useful Jellyfin apps that make my self-hosted server so much better
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I run a Jellyfin server on an HP ProDesk 600 G6 in my home lab, under Proxmox with iGPU passed through for hardware transcoding. With the server side sorted, the app on each device decides how Jellyfin feels. Though the official clients work just fine, a handful of third-party clients include things I’d otherwise chase with a plugin or workaround.

After trying a bunch of apps, I settled on four Jellyfin apps that I usually install first. All of them work with Jellyfin 12 and are client apps, not server plugins, so the features are baked into the app.

Infuse cuts down subtitle hunting

A one-tap OpenSubtitles fetch and Trakt sync

Even though I have a humble library, it does have several titles without subtitles embedded or included alongside them. Fixing that in Jellyfin’s web client means digging through the subtitle search, then picking one, and hoping it sticks. Infuse does this inside the media player with a single tap, and it pulls the subtitle from OpenSubtitles for free.

Trakt synced my watch history and ratings with my account without a server plugin. Infuse can also skip intros and credits using IntroDB. However, I’d install it for easy subtitle fetching. It also treats Jellyfin as one of the several sources to map a media server or network shares, so I can use Infuse to browse a NAS or a Plex server too.

Firecore, the developers of Infuse, added Jellyfin 12 support in version 8.5.2, so I had to update the client before pointing it to a Jellyfin server. The only catch with Infuse is that it’s limited to Apple hardware: iPhone, iPad, Apple TV, and Mac. The app is free to download, but Infuse Pro costs $2/month, $17/year, or $100 for a lifetime license.

Infuse
See at Apple

Wholphin switches the resolution and the refresh rate automatically

PIN-protected profiles and the ability to skip settings

Wholphin is a free Jellyfin app for Android TV and Fire TV written from scratch, and I ran it on my Fire TV Stick 4K. It plays the videos through ExoPlayer or MPV. I like it because it switches my TV’s refresh rate and resolution to match what I’m watching without changing any settings. I noticed that right after moving over from an Apple TV 4K.

I can lock the profiles I created behind a PIN, which works great on the TV I share with my family. I can also rearrange the home page rows and pin collections, genres, or studios to make navigating with the Fire TV remote easier.

Wholphin lets me skip intros and credits sequences automatically, or it can show me a prompt. But it reads those segments from the server, so a segment provider such as the Intro Skipper plugin has to generate them first. I installed it on my Jellyfin server. Wholphin only decides what happens once that data exists. Subtitle search works the same way and needs a compatible subtitle plugin on the server.

Wholphin
OS
Android TV
See at Github See at Google Play Store

Fladder pulls a server dashboard inside a client

Check sessions and run tasks without poking through the web UI

Most clients stop at playback, but Fladder goes a step ahead and shows who’s streaming from the Jellyfin server and how far along they are. But this is buried in the Control Panel under Settings. That’s where I manage users, libraries, and scheduled tasks. Sometimes I use Tailscale for remote access, and checking the server status from the phone instead of a full browser is quite convenient.

Unfortunately, it doesn’t replace Jellyfin’s Playback Reporting plugin, since the panel shows live sessions, not the user’s full viewing history. That means no log or chart of what got viewed last month, just “who’s watching what.”

For requests, I integrated Seerr into Fladder, and the app has its own settings for skipping intros and credits. The app’s interface looks the same on Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android. There is a minor difference from the native feel, and I’m fine with that. Wholphin is open source and also has a Docker image.

Fladder
OS
Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, Android TV
See at Github See at Google Play Store

Findroid keeps your library playable offline

Direct play only, without an option to adjust bitrate

As a native Android app, Findroid follows Google’s Material design language. I like it because I can download movies and shows for offline playback. The app earns its spot on my Android device since those downloads work in a dead zone, on a flight, or anywhere the server isn’t reachable.

Findroid uses mpv for playback and renders subtitles properly. It uses Jellyfin’s Media Segments API to skip intros, credits, and outros. Of course, I had to install the Intro Skipper plugin on the server for that.

Findroid
OS
Android
See at Github See at Google Play Store

Findroid only supports direct play, and transcoding isn’t possible. Even though Jellyfin could use the iGPU passthrough on Proxmox for hardware transcoding, Findroid never asks for that. So I can’t pick a streaming bitrate, even when using the app on a weaker connection. That said, the offline downloads make up for this. Findroid is free on Google Play and F-Droid.

5 tips for managing your Jellyfin server to make your life easier

Spruce up Jellyfin to make it work as your personal streaming service

2
By  Samir Makwana

Pick the client that fits the screen you plan to use

None of these apps replace each other, and that’s the point. Infuse covers Apple devices, Wholphin covers Android TV and Fire TV, Fladder covers computers and doubles as a dashboard, and Findroid covers Android devices. Just remember that Wholphin and Findroid need an extra server plugin to skip the intros and credits. Infuse Pro is the only paid piece, and the other three take a few minutes to set up.

item.title: Claude finally got me to stop procrastinating, and it only took one instruction
item.itunes:title: Claude finally got me to stop procrastinating, and it only took one instruction
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Procrastination is one of the problems that the productivity world seems to keep throwing software at, promising to fix your life for good. To-do apps and planners have been at this for years, and now AI assistants are in on it too, with many happy to schedule your entire week for you. You might have already come across one or two tools that genuinely helped manage your time and track your productivity - most of these tools have something good to offer, and there's something out there for everyone.

The problem is there are just so many to keep track of that the tools become yet another thing to procrastinate on, and AI assistants often inflate the issue by giving you a breakdown with a million steps in an attempt to seem helpful. But I've managed to reel my AI back in with one simple instruction.

Want to stay in the loop with the latest in AI? The XDA AI Insider newsletter drops weekly with deep dives, tool recommendations, and hands-on coverage you won't find anywhere else on the site. Subscribe by modifying your newsletter preferences!

AI assistants can make procrastination worse

A 12-step plan only feels productive, until it isn't

Ask Claude to help you start pretty much anything and you'll get a plan back, usually with headers and a checklist that has its own smaller checklists underneath. It feels productive for about two minutes, and then I just close the tab because now the task looks bigger than it did before I asked.

A lot of it is just how models are tuned. Anthropic's prompting docs for Opus 5 point out that its default responses run longer than earlier Opus models did. My first instinct was to drop the effort setting, which didn't really change anything, and the docs actually explain why. Effort changes how much the model thinks before it answers, and turning it down won't reliably make its responses shorter, more concise, or get to the point. This leaves you with instructions as your only option to reel it in.

There's also the bigger issue that Claude only knows about whatever you bring to it, and I'm rarely going to bring the thing I'm avoiding - that's sort of the whole point of procrastination. What I needed was something that wouldn't plan anything and would go looking for that task by itself, without me pointing at it first.

The Claude feature everyone ignores is the one I use every single day to boost my productivity

The ultimate Claude power-user trick

2
By  Parth Shah

Breaking down the instruction that got Claude to help me stop procrastinating

Every sentence is there to shut down a habit

The instruction itself is short and simple: "Don't give me a plan. Tell me which task here I've been avoiding the longest, and give me one step I can finish in the next 5 minutes. Then stop."

The first sentence goes after the default behavior, but it probably wouldn't hold up alone, since Anthropic's prompting guidance notes Claude does better with a description of what you want than a list of what you don't - so it needs the rest of the instruction to actually work.

The second sentence gives it a job. "Avoiding the longest" makes Claude go and find the answer rather than wait for me to name something I'd obviously never name myself. And it has to work that out from whatever it can see inside the folder, which means it's going to look for stuff that's been sitting half-completed. Sometimes file dates can be misleading, so I add a little caveat to ignore that file data and Claude defaults to ranking importance based on what's actually in the file.

The 5-minute step works as a stopping condition, which lines up with Anthropic's Opus 5.5 advice to spell out what done looks like and when to stop. "Then stop" plays into how literally newer Claude models take instructions, and I locked the output to a couple of lines too.

I turned Claude into my productivity command center with these tools

Claude gets better with the right tools.

2
By  Parth Shah

Where the instruction lives

And which version of Claude reads it best

Claude Code has a feature called skills, which are instruction files it can load when a task seems relevant, or when you call one by name. I set up a skill for this instruction and it's called "nudge", and setting disable-model-invocation to true stops Claude from loading it on its own, so it only runs when I type /nudge.

I also have a "junk" folder now where all my half-baked ideas and half-finished tasks go to live, so basically every side project, priority project I've been putting off, and anything I'm still actively learning. And this skill looks at this folder by default. I did consider a CLAUDE.md instead, but that gets read at the start of every session in the folder, and I didn't want every conversation opening with a guilt trip.

Regular Claude Chat gets my life admin. I put the same instruction in some of my Project instructions where I keep things like therapy progress, workouts, goals, and so on. There are no file dates in a chat, so it works from what I've uploaded and told it, and it still lands on whatever I keep skipping. Pasting it from a notes file works too.

I ran the identical /nudge on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, both at medium effort. Both picked the same file and step, then stopped where they were told to. Opus read all seven files one by one, while Sonnet searched the folder and ran a single command.

I'd say Sonnet 5.5 is probably what I'll keep using for this because it seems to suit tasks with a clear spec and a way to check the result, which this whole instruction basically is. Opus 5.5 is a safe pick too, with cloud storage company Box, one of Anthropic's early testers, reporting answers that were 40% less verbose than Opus 5 with no accuracy loss. I reckon Opus 5's default length would fight the instruction, and Haiku would probably follow the format but be worse at judging what's most avoided. Medium effort seems like plenty either way.

I thought I knew Claude until I discovered these 5 productivity workflows

My Claude setup finally makes sense.

1
By  Parth Shah

It doesn't make me more productive, it just helps me start

My junk folder isn't going to get any smaller any time soon, but it's not supposed to. The difference is that I actually open it now because I know I'll get one small, manageable thing back instead of an entire plan with a million components. It's already helped me set up one meeting I've been avoiding, do one audit of something important, and fact-check some details of one of my short stories.

Claude

item.title: Pangolin lets me reach my own apps from anywhere, and I didn't have to open a single port
item.itunes:title: Pangolin lets me reach my own apps from anywhere, and I didn't have to open a single port
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have two internet connections for my homelab, but neither gives me a simple path for incoming traffic. Both are behind CGNAT, which makes traditional hole-punching on my router difficult. For my homelab, where I have many apps that need public access, my redundant internet setup doesn't help at all. After running back and forth looking for a solution, I finally settled on Pangolin, and here's what changed.

I couldn't open a port even if I wanted to

Two ISPs. Neither would let me in.

I live in the countryside, and though it has many perks over a metro city, it comes with a few downsides as well. One of the downsides is that I have a limited number of ISPs available for the internet, and most of them are local.

For my homelab, I have subscribed to two ISPs. Why two? Because of a smaller number of users, the connection is generally stable, and outages are rare. But if the connection is down for some reason, the outage typically lasts 12 to 24 hours, or longer if it is a weekend. The second connection helps keep the homelab up when the primary is down.

But the more concerning thing is that both the connections are behind CGNAT. That means each shares a carrier-side public IP, which isn’t publicly accessible from the internet. And behind CGNAT, there is no traditional way to forward any port from the router.

Even if inbound access were available for me, I wasn’t interested in making my home router the public-facing entry point for multiple homelab services. There are multiple services on my homelab that I never want to be accessible from the internet, like admin dashboards.

But there are a few services that need public access. Immich, Jellyfin, and Nextcloud are among the most used services in my homelab, and I use them even when I am away. Since traditional port forwarding wasn’t an option for me, I needed something to establish the connection outward from my network.

I built an always‑on VPN gateway with a Raspberry Pi Zero to access my home lab from anywhere

It's perfect when I want to work on my home lab projects from external networks

12
By  Ayush Pande

How Pangolin gets around it

My server calls out. My router hears nothing.

Pangolin helps me reach my self-hosted services from anywhere in the world without relying on an inbound connection to my home internet. Let me be clear before you jump to the comments section and say I could have just used Cloudflare Tunnel. I have used it in the past, and why I replaced Cloudflare Tunnel with Pangolin is a whole different story I've already told.

Pangolin has three major components — Newt, Gerbil, and Traefik. Newt runs on my home server and is used to connect my homelab to the Pangolin control plane for establishing the outbound connection. Pangolin itself is hosted on a VPS, since it requires a public IP. Gerbil builds a secure, encrypted tunnel using WireGuard, and Traefik routes the traffic to the appropriate application it requested.

Internet -> VPS -> Traefik -> Gerbil/tunnel -> Newt -> app.

The Pangolin control plane handles all the tedious jobs under the hood. And my CGNAT connections don’t care about the whole process because the traffic never directly hits my router.

There were a few snags that I faced while setting up the service for the first time; for example, Newt and the service had to share the same Docker network, but that’s just how Docker works. But it is a one-time thing, so once set up, I didn’t have to look back.

But as mentioned earlier, not all my services need to be publicly accessible. There are many services, such as Portainer and AdGuard Home, that are only meant for me. So, for those types of services, I access them with a private mesh VPN like NetBird and Tailscale. With Pangolin and NetBird, I am covered from both ends, and the best part is I don’t have any inbound ports on my router.

Pangolin

Self-hosted, open-source for exposing your own services under your own domain.

See at Github See at Official Site

What living with it is actually like

It's just another URL. That's also the catch.

The important question is how it works after the initial one-time setup. Honestly, I don’t open the Pangolin dashboard every day, and that is the best outcome. For example, while I am traveling and need some documents urgently, I just open Nextcloud in the browser using the public domain name, and I download them. It is as simple as that. I don’t need to worry about the underlying tunnel or the home network. It behaves like any other web service.

Adding a new service to Pangolin takes less than 30 seconds. Once I am done deploying a new service on my homelab, and if it needs to be publicly accessible, I open the Pangolin dashboard and add it as a new public resource by using just a few basic details. The new resource name, subdomain, and local IP address with its port. Done.

But there are a few downsides to this setup if you are thinking of setting it up in your homelab. The first and most important one is that it is not free. The Pangolin service itself is free, but it requires a VPS with a public IP to work, and renting a VPS is another recurring expense.

For me, all internet traffic first goes to Germany and then reaches my home server. Why Germany? Because my VPS’s public endpoint is in Nuremberg, as it is cost-effective. Personally, a few ms delay isn’t a big tradeoff, but if you host services where each ms is crucial, then you will have to rent a VPS near your location.

Since a VPS is a piece of infrastructure owned by someone else and you just rent it, it becomes another dependency; if you miss a bill or the host faces an outage, it directly affects your homelab’s remote access.

And if you see it security-wise, even though my home server isn’t directly exposed, the services are still publicly reachable, so a few further steps are needed to make it more secure. I personally use Pocket ID for SSO wherever applicable and put CrowdSec at the front for edge protection.

I used this self-hosted tool to scan my network, and it's surprisingly powerful

Reconya gives you real-time visibility into every device on your network.

8
By  Dhruv Bhutani

The trade-off I'm happy to live with

Pangolin offers a simple way out of the CGNAT wall for someone who wants normal URLs for their self-hosted services without relying on a client being installed on every device. But it is not universally the right fit. If you are happy with a mesh VPN for private access, then you are already good. But if you want a publicly accessible HTTPS URL for your services without any unnecessary overhead, and you can live with the VPS cost and another dependency, Pangolin is worth a try.

item.itunes:title: Transform your laptop into a beastly workstation with this 12-in-1 dock that's just $42
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
This Baseus 12-in-1 docking station adds ports to your laptop, expanding its capabilities. It's a must-have accessory if you rely on your laptop for work and personal use. The good news is that it doesn't cost as much as you would think, with Amazon dropping the price down to just $42. The 19% discount isn't huge, but it is the best price we've seen on this product.

Baseus Laptop Docking Station
USB Power Delivery
Yes
Power supply included
No
Max display res.
4K
HDMI
Yes
Ethernet
Yes
See at Amazon

An easy one to pick up

It's not often you see a 12-in-1 docking station that costs just $42. But here we are, and we're thankful that Baseus makes such a product. The most vital part of an expansion device is the ports. And this one has some good ones.

You get one 3.5mm audio jack, USB-C for data, three USB-A ports, an SD and microSD card reader, Ethernet, DisplayPort, two HDMI ports, and a USB-C 100W PD port for power. That's twelve total, and many you won't find on current laptops.

While you can display on multiple monitors, you'll get better support if you use a Windows product. You can output to multiple monitors with a Mac, but you'll only get one extension. With Windows, you can set a different screen for each monitor, up to three.

Of course, while this product is aimed at laptops, you can also use it for a desktop, PC gaming console, phone, or tablet. As long as the device is compatible, it should support all the ports. You're getting a lot here with this docking station.

item.title: DLSS 5 is the new ray tracing, and it's going to be inescapable soon
item.itunes:title: DLSS 5 is the new ray tracing, and it's going to be inescapable soon
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When Nvidia unveiled DLSS 5 to the world at GTC in March 2026, it pitched it as its most significant graphics breakthrough since real-time ray tracing. Much of the headlines were dominated by the uncanny image previews and "DLSS 5 ON" memes, but that opening line said more about Nvidia's plans for the technology than anything it has talked about since. Ray tracing launched as a premium feature that came with a steep performance cost, had sparse adoption at launch, and if you had a GTX 1080 Ti, you couldn't run it properly because it didn't have the RT cores to do so.

Just a few short years later, ray tracing became a hard requirement, and most enthusiasts on a Pascal card have long since upgraded. While the neural rendering tech that it's based on doesn't have a new hardware requirement and the adoption is even thinner when compared to ray tracing's introduction, it does have a very steep performance cost, and I wouldn't be shocked if its inescapable in a matter of a couple of years.

DLSS 4.5 is expensive, but it’s the best thing to happen to my aging RTX PC

The upside is remarkable, but the cost isn't equal for all.

19
By  Samarveer Singh

Nvidia has run this playbook before

Their "significant graphics breakthroughs" usually come with an upgrade tax

Turing introduced ray tracing to every gamer's vernacular, but it came with so many other meaningful changes that, in retrospect, were pretty monumental for Nvidia. It renamed the product line, and ray tracing became the face of Nvidia's gaming brand. While the hard cutoff for GTX hardware was real, every feature since followed a similar playbook.

Nvidia would release a DLSS generation, make the headline feature an exclusive to the newest generation of cards, and then follow up with support for the other features for the older generations a bit later. Frame Generation launched as an RTX 40 exclusive, and DLSS 4 made Multi Frame Generation exclusive to RTX 50 while RTX 40 kept the older Frame Generation. DLSS 5 is no different.

It launched on September 3 in NBA 2K27, limited to RTX 50 GPUs GeForce Now. Nvidia has since said it will expand support to RTX 40 once RTX 50 performance is more fully tuned, but hasn't given a date, and perhaps most importantly, it has made no commitment for RTX 30 or older cards.

4 reasons why Nvidia's DLSS is ruining PC gaming

DLSS works like magic, but it's actually making your games worse

47
By  Hamlin Rozario

The basis for a baked-in requirement is there

Neural rendering doesn't have any new hardware requirements yet, but it can if Nvidia wants it to

DLSS 5 is currently just an Nvidia model applied on top of an already rendered frame, and as of right now, it's a toggle that players can choose to turn on and off. People have even managed to get it running on Radeon GPUs, so there's no current secret sauce that locks it to Nvidia-only, at least in any serious capacity.

Ray tracing didn't become mandatory because of the RTX brand, either. It became mandatory because DXR and Vulkan gave developers a vendor-neutral way to target it, and the current consoles shipped with hardware to run it. That's why Indiana Jones and the Great Circle requires hardware ray tracing at every preset, and why Doom: The Dark Ages locks out anything older than the RTX 20 and RX 6000 series.

The good news is that neural rendering has already had its DXR moment with AMD, Nvidia, Intel and Qualcomm committing to officially supporting DirectX Shader Model 6.9, which introduces Cooperative Vectors, letting shaders run small neural networks inline. This is the layer that could be baked into games, like the neural texturing, materials, and lighting caches. With that said, there's nothing stopping Nvidia from drawing lines within its own lineup as they've done previously.

DLSS 5 uses the FP8 format, which is why Ada's tensor cores can run it and why RTX 40 support is coming at all. A future version built around a newer number format, or a heavier model that leans on shader-level tensor access, would leave older cards technically capable but officially unsupported. Older GeForce cards already allegedly go through slower CUDA or compute shader paths to reach their tensor cores from inside shaders, and that's sort of a hard requirement in and of itself. RTX 50 owners are getting DLSS 5 as it exists today, with no guarantee they'll get the version that matters once it stops being optional.

3 features RTX 40 owners are getting in the wake of the RTX 50

It's not all about the new generation.

5
By  Simon Batt

Why DLSS 5 could stay optional

RT was way less polarizing

While the consensus on ray tracing was that it enhanced the fidelity of most rendered scenes at a heavy performance cost, DLSS 5 has a much more polarizing reputation already, and it's not even widely available yet.

It completely changes the way a scene looks, with the most jarring differences coming from the facial features of characters. Whether you think it actually enhances the image is completely subjective at the moment, and the performance cost of turning it on might not be worth sacrificing other settings—ray tracing would be one of the first things you'd turn off to save performance headroom for DLSS, ironically enough.

7 older GPUs that still hold their own against the RTX 50 series

Most gamers are considering upgrading, but only those without these GPUs.

41
By  Samarveer Singh

What this means if you're buying a new GPU

Ray tracing showed how this goes. A premium feature launches on one generation, the industry builds a standard around it, consoles adopt the hardware, and then the requirement is set. It definitely doesn't mean you should run out and buy an RTX 5090 tomorrow, but it does mean you might be in for an upgrade sooner rather than later.

There's a catch for early adopters, too. RTX 20 owners bought first-generation ray tracing hardware, and by the time ray tracing was common, the entry-level RTX 2060 couldn't handle it in modern games even at 1080p. RTX 50 is first-generation DLSS 5 hardware. When neural rendering stops being optional, today's early adopters could find themselves in the same position.

item.title: VLC was painfully slow on my Windows 11 PC until I found what was throttling it
item.itunes:title: VLC was painfully slow on my Windows 11 PC until I found what was throttling it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
VLC is perhaps the only media player I've used consistently ever since Windows Media Player stopped being the one-stop video destination on my PC. Most of you reading this are probably in the same boat. VLC even has advanced tricks up its sleeve that most users never get around to. There's a reason it's still the most popular media player on Windows, and PCs in general.

So, you can understand my frustration when VLC started misbehaving around a month ago. Whenever I launched a video, the media player took unusually long to open. When I looked up the issue online, I found that Microsoft Defender is the culprit, thanks to a faulty Windows update released in August.

After 20 years together, VLC and I are finally breaking up, and it's because of this app

I might never see the orange cone again

6
By  Samarveer Singh

VLC was testing my nerves over the past few weeks

Even a reinstall didn't fix the slow launch time

I use VLC fairly regularly. Whether it's watching my smartphone videos or local media on my PC, VLC has been integrated into my lifestyle for decades now. So, when it started launching abnormally slowly a few weeks ago, sometimes even taking around 15 seconds, I was naturally annoyed. I hadn't changed anything on my end, so my frustration was naturally directed toward VideoLan.

At first, I thought a new version was at fault, but there had been no updates in August, when this problem started. I reinstalled VLC to fix whatever background shenanigans were messing things up, but the problem didn't really go away. Moreover, my Windows 11 PC was experiencing other issues related to File Explorer, so I attributed the slow VLC launch time to my troubled Windows installation. It was only after Googling the issue that I found the real culprit.

6 lightweight tools I install before anything else on a new PC

You shouldn't live without these

1
By  João Carrasqueira

Microsoft Defender has been slowing VLC down

Who would have thought?

The internet was quick to blame VideoLan, with some users even blaming Microsoft for deliberately slowing the media player down. On August 12, however, the VideoLan team themselves pointed to a bug in one of the Microsoft Defender updates, which made the security suite quarantine VLC's plug-in cache. I only found out about this after an article took me to the concerned X post by VideoLan.

Indeed, it was shown that a recent Microsoft Defender update and the Windows KB5121003 update were responsible for this mess. I should have blamed Microsoft, considering how many Windows updates this year have been faulty. The plugins.dat file ending up in Windows quarantine was slowing down VLC launch times around the world, which is certainly one of the more bizarre Windows fails.

Windows 10's forced updates: A history of disastrous consequences

These Windows 10 updates promised improvements but delivered chaos instead

By  Joe Rice-Jones

Microsoft hasn't fixed it yet, but you can do it yourself

Surprise, surprise!

At the time of writing, Microsoft has not released a patch to resolve the Defender bug wreaking havoc on VLC. That said, you can do a few things yourself to restore your VLC launch speed. For starters, you should regenerate the VLC cache affected by Microsoft Defender. You can either reinstall the media player to reset everything along with the cache or run VLC media player - reset preferences and cache files by typing "vlc" in the Windows search bar.

Note that this doesn't prevent Microsoft Defender from putting the VLC cache back into quarantine. So, you also need to add an exclusion for your VLC directory in the Virus & threat protection settings. Using the Exclusions section, you can simply point to the installed VideoLAN or VLC folder on your PC, so that Defender stops scanning it. While this isn't the ideal way to fix this problem, it's the best one we've got for now.

If you're still on Windows 10, switching to a new antivirus won't be enough

Windows 10 will continue receiving antivirus updates, but that's only half the protection

2
By  Tanveer Singh

Windows updates have had an awful reputation lately

It seems Microsoft messes up more than it fixes with Windows updates. Sometimes, it's unexpected BSODs or deleted user files, and sometimes, it's boot loops or broken VPN configurations. This time, it's the false quarantining of VLC's plug-in cache, causing slow launch times for millions of users. Thankfully, despite no official patch from Microsoft, users can easily fix the problem themselves.

item.title: A box of cheap sensors taught me more about the ESP32 than any tutorial
item.itunes:title: A box of cheap sensors taught me more about the ESP32 than any tutorial
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I got my first ESP32, tutorials were the first thing I consulted, and they worked well for the most part. If I wanted to build a Bluetooth proxy, I’d look into official and community posts on how to do so. Likewise, I’d check on common projects I could build with these tiny microcontrollers, and pick up the sensor, circuitry, and robotics modules accordingly. Although this methodical approach helped me build cool smart home gizmos, I didn’t really learn anything about the ESP32 during the projects.

In fact, I’d spent quite a long time working on random DIY ESP32 tutorials, but I still had no idea how this microcontroller lineup worked. So, I decided to pick up a cheap 37-in-1 sensor kit and go full-throttle on my experiments. And I must say, that decision is single-handedly the reason I was able to familiarize myself with the ins-and-outs of my pint-sized companion.

4 simple ESP32 projects you can build without any sensors

Not all ESP32 projects need to involve extra sensors or circuit components

By  Ayush Pande

Random sensors helped me get better at making ESP32 projects

After all, following a tutorial didn’t require any effort on my end

Before you call me out about my stance against online ESP32 guides and tutorials, let me add that they’re a solid option when you’re trying to build functional projects. But the biggest issue with these curated projects is that everything from the sensor connections to the code has been tailor-made to work perfectly. So, the chances of things going wrong mid-project are fairly low, and that’s somewhat detrimental when you’re trying to get some hands-on experience with an ESP32.

Meanwhile, attempting to build something barely-functional with random sensors removes the training wheels and the hand-holding aspects of curated projects. For example, the KY-037 module in my sensor kit caught my attention as soon as I bought the collection. But without any tutorial telling me what to do, I had to figure things out on my own. Once I’d looked into it a bit more, I realized it could detect high-sensitivity sounds, but I still had no clue how I could pair it with my microcontroller. So, I began reading the documentation on ESPBoards, instead of just following tutorials blindly.

The same goes for the KY-012 active buzzer, KY-002 vibration sensor, and KY-008 laser module. I also received some much-needed experience with the analog, I2C, SPI, and other communication standards this way, which I never quite noticed when I was busy following 20-minute-long videos on building specific projects.

7 ESP32 projects that replaced commercial smart home gadgets in my house with cheaper, local hardware

These are the commercial products I've replaced with ESP32-powered variants.

11
By  Adam Conway

I’ve grown accustomed to the ESP32 pinout thanks to my sensor kits

I no longer panic when a tutorial doesn’t include the GPIO pin layout

Another neat aspect of learning everything by experimenting with random sensors was that I’d started to get familiar with the way the ESP32 pins work. Of course, I still need to look up the pinout diagram for my tiny tinkering companion while working on DIY sensor setups. But what I did learn were the capabilities of the GPIO pins. In the past, if I wanted to build a vibration sensor from a tutorial, I’d try to find the connection diagrams for the power, ground, and signal ports, and freak out if the exact pin configuration on the website/video didn't match my specific board.

Now? I’d just open the ESP32 pinout and realize that GPIO 4, 16, and 19 would work with the KY-002, as they’re flexible enough to support digital readings from the sensor. Likewise, if I wanted to use the I2C protocol for, say, a weather sensor like the BME280, I’d immediately recognize that GPIO 21 could accommodate the data signals and GPIO 22 could provide the clock sync as soon as I see the SDA and SCL icons next to them, respectively.

So, if the pin layouts on a tutorial don’t match the ones I’ve got on my ESP32, I’d look at what protocol the sensor uses, go through the ESP32 pin diagram, and connect the two together with just this much information instead of scouring through other tutorials trying to get the exact configuration as my ESP32 clones.

Thanks to their cheap price tags, I wouldn’t be in trouble if I broke things

I don’t need to watch my every move when I tinker with my ESP32 sensors

The best part about starting with sensor kits instead of following full-fledged tutorials is that even if things go south, you won’t end up losing a lot of money. My ESP32 was roughly $10, and my box of sensors cost about twice as much. That’s not a lot of money, especially if you compare it to other “cheap” devices in the tech ecosystem like mini-PCs or Raspberry Pis. Let’s say I broke a random light-detection sensor by accidentally connecting it to the 5V pin instead of its 3.3V counterpart. I can just order a new one for a few dollars, instead of spending dozens of bucks on an expensive replacement.

This makes ESP32 projects extremely cheap to tinker with, and that’s low-key why I was able to learn from my mistakes and experiment to my heart’s content worrying about botched components.

ESP32 experiments are pretty simple if I stick to ESPHome

When I first got the idea of training my ESP32 muscle with random sensors, I immediately shut it down because I was afraid of the extra difficulty of figuring things on my own without a step-by-step guide. But contrary to what I expected, tinkering with ESP32 sensors is fairly straightforward, and it’s all thanks to ESPHome.

Rather than pasting long C++ code into the Arduino IDE while following tutorials, I can just write a few snippets of YAML syntax on ESPHome and watch my sensors react to the code within a few seconds. The DIY ESP32 + sensor combos created via ESPHome also integrate into Home Assistant as typical devices, so I get some tangible benefits from my creations instead of just novelty projects that I’d disassemble days after I build them.

item.title: Jellyfin's setup complexity is why Plex still charges $7 a month and gets away with it
item.itunes:title: Jellyfin's setup complexity is why Plex still charges $7 a month and gets away with it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When it comes to self-hosting your own media, Plex is undoubtedly the household name, and rightly so. It may be a paid commercial service, but it's also the easiest to operate, and the one with the least friction involved.

On the other hand, its open-source alternative, Jellyfin, remains the "power-user choice." Jellyfin has undeniably improved over the years, and tremendously so, and I'd daresay it's ready for prime time.

And yet, the elephant in the room remains — you still have to set it all up yourself, which, when it comes to FOSS (Free and Open Source Software) is par for the course. Sadly, it's also why millions still swear by Plex, and continue spending money to stream their own media files across their own networks.

I stopped choosing between Plex and Jellyfin, and my media server is better because of it

Both Plex and Jellyfin are better when you stop trying to choose between them

19
By  Samarveer Singh

Jellyfin has every feature you need

But you still need to set them all up yourself

Just because Plex asks for $6.99 a month for the Plex Pass doesn't mean that it automatically has the better feature set than Jellyfin. In fact, with the right collection of plugins, a Jellyfin media server can become much more robust than a vanilla Plex server. Effectively speaking, there is no feature in the paid Plex Pass that Jellyfin doesn't offer for free. There is, of course, a catch, though.

From finding and installing the right plugin to setting up port forwarding or familiarizing yourself with Tailscale to share your media server with your friends, Jellyfin demands that you learn and set it up all by yourself. If you need hardware transcoding on your server, you have to enable it yourself, much like HDR-to-SDR tone mapping and other crucial features that make or break any media server.

Plex Pass costs $6.99 per month, $69.99 per year, or $749.99 for lifetime access.

The plugins, of course, are where much of the initial friction comes from. You can't simply throw $7 at the screen and get metadata, playback history, auto-subtitles, intro skipping, trailers, or custom themes. Instead, you have to find the right plugin for yourself and add it to your server manually.

Admitted, all of the "work" involved in setting up a Jellyfin server comes rather easily for the initiated, but for those new to self-hosting, Jellyfin can be surprisingly intimidating during their first week.

Plex Pass is expensive, but it's the only streaming app my family actually uses

I like simplicity in my life and my family agrees

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Jellyfin's biggest strength is also its weakness

Friction remains the biggest deal-breaker in 2026

Anyone who is put off by Jellyfin's initially barebones structure would naturally complain about the complexity involved. Ironically, that complexity only exists because Jellyfin refuses to make your choices for you. Where Plex hides the "boring" administrative stuff behind a polished interface, Jellyfin willingly exposes it for you to choose your metadata providers, subtitle sources, transcoding behavior, remote-access method, library structure, and practically everything else.

Once you do know what you're doing, it's exactly this freedom that feels fantastic. Hardware transcoding becomes a feature you can use from your own GPU. You can even choose not to expose your server to the internet and instead use Tailscale. Even if you want to completely redesign the interface, there's probably a plug for exactly what you're looking for.

Plex makes you a customer first and an administrator second, while Jellyfin hands you the keys to the kingdom from the get-go.

It's exactly these features that appear as too many knobs for newcomers. Understanding Direct Play versus transcoding, figuring out why HDR content suddenly looks washed out, or realizing that your server needs hardware acceleration enabled before it stops hammering the CPU can turn what should be a media server into a surprisingly educational weekend project.

That, ladies and gentlemen, is the Jellyfin trade-off. Plex makes you a customer first, and an administrator second, if that. Conversely, Jellyfin makes you the administrator from the moment you download it and open up the dashboard. Once it's all configured, there's nothing quite like the control you get with Jellyfin. Getting there, however, requires some earning.

Plex becomes incredibly hard to justify once Jellyfin is up and running

The hard part is learning the ins and outs of your own server

With a Jellyfin server, once the libraries are configured, metadata is sorted, transcoding is working, and remote access is taken care of, the server largely disappears into the background. Mine has reached the point where I rarely think about it at all. Oh, and it doesn't sip $6.99 every month from my bank account.

Plex still has an advantage when other people are involved, though. I can hand a Plex account to someone who has never heard the words "Direct Play" or "hardware transcoding," and they can generally figure it out themselves. Jellyfin can offer a similarly polished experience, but getting someone there may require a small amount of tech support.

And that, more than any missing feature, is why Plex remains so difficult to displace. Jellyfin can become an exceptional media platform once you've built it properly, but Plex's greatest trick is making the person using your server completely unaware that there is a server behind it.

iOS compatible
Yes
Android compatible
Yes
Desktop compatible
Yes

Jellyfin is one of the best Plex alternatives you can get, and that's thanks to its open-source nature and powerful set of features. There are apps for basically every platform and it's completely free to run your very own server.

See at Jellyfin Jellyfin 12 (RC5)
Jellyfin finally feels good on my TV, but I had to stop using the default client

Wholphin is the Jellyfin client Android TV should have shipped with.

14
By  Samarveer Singh

The friction is becoming harder to justify

I don't think Jellyfin needs to become Plex to win people over. That would actually undermine much of what makes it appealing in the first place. What it needs is to make the first few hours less intimidating, especially for someone who has never touched a self-hosted application before.

Every time I use Jellyfin right now, the gap between a "power-user project" and a genuinely mainstream media server gets smaller. I do completely understand why someone would pay for Plex, but Jellyfin increasingly feels less like an alternative for enthusiasts, and more like a polished and sensible choice that simply asks a little more elbow grease upfront.

I do completely understand why someone would pay for Plex, but Jellyfin increasingly feels less like an alternative for enthusiasts, and more like a polished and sensible choice that simply asks a little more elbow grease upfront.

When it comes to self-hosting your own media, Plex is undoubtedly the household name, and rightly so. It may be a paid commercial service, but it's also the easiest to operate, and the one with the least friction involved.

On the other hand, its open-source alternative, Jellyfin, remains the "power-user choice." Jellyfin has undeniably improved over the years, and tremendously so, and I'd daresay it's ready for prime time.

And yet, the elephant in the room remains — you still have to set it all up yourself, which, when it comes to FOSS (Free and Open Source Software) is par for the course. Sadly, it's also why millions still swear by Plex, and continue spending money to stream their own media files across their own networks.

I stopped choosing between Plex and Jellyfin, and my media server is better because of it

Both Plex and Jellyfin are better when you stop trying to choose between them

19
By  Samarveer Singh

Jellyfin has every feature you need

But you still need to set them all up yourself

Just because Plex asks for $6.99 a month for the Plex Pass doesn't mean that it automatically has the better feature set than Jellyfin. In fact, with the right collection of plugins, a Jellyfin media server can become much more robust than a vanilla Plex server. Effectively speaking, there is no feature in the paid Plex Pass that Jellyfin doesn't offer for free. There is, of course, a catch, though.

From finding and installing the right plugin to setting up port forwarding or familiarizing yourself with Tailscale to share your media server with your friends, Jellyfin demands that you learn and set it up all by yourself. If you need hardware transcoding on your server, you have to enable it yourself, much like HDR-to-SDR tone mapping and other crucial features that make or break any media server.

Plex Pass costs $6.99 per month, $69.99 per year, or $749.99 for lifetime access.

The plugins, of course, are where much of the initial friction comes from. You can't simply throw $7 at the screen and get metadata, playback history, auto-subtitles, intro skipping, trailers, or custom themes. Instead, you have to find the right plugin for yourself and add it to your server manually.

Admitted, all of the "work" involved in setting up a Jellyfin server comes rather easily for the initiated, but for those new to self-hosting, Jellyfin can be surprisingly intimidating during their first week.

Plex Pass is expensive, but it's the only streaming app my family actually uses

I like simplicity in my life and my family agrees

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Jellyfin's biggest strength is also its weakness

Friction remains the biggest deal-breaker in 2026

Anyone who is put off by Jellyfin's initially barebones structure would naturally complain about the complexity involved. Ironically, that complexity only exists because Jellyfin refuses to make your choices for you. Where Plex hides the "boring" administrative stuff behind a polished interface, Jellyfin willingly exposes it for you to choose your metadata providers, subtitle sources, transcoding behavior, remote-access method, library structure, and practically everything else.

Once you do know what you're doing, it's exactly this freedom that feels fantastic. Hardware transcoding becomes a feature you can use from your own GPU. You can even choose not to expose your server to the internet and instead use Tailscale. Even if you want to completely redesign the interface, there's probably a plug for exactly what you're looking for.

Plex makes you a customer first and an administrator second, while Jellyfin hands you the keys to the kingdom from the get-go.

It's exactly these features that appear as too many knobs for newcomers. Understanding Direct Play versus transcoding, figuring out why HDR content suddenly looks washed out, or realizing that your server needs hardware acceleration enabled before it stops hammering the CPU can turn what should be a media server into a surprisingly educational weekend project.

That, ladies and gentlemen, is the Jellyfin trade-off. Plex makes you a customer first, and an administrator second, if that. Conversely, Jellyfin makes you the administrator from the moment you download it and open up the dashboard. Once it's all configured, there's nothing quite like the control you get with Jellyfin. Getting there, however, requires some earning.

Plex becomes incredibly hard to justify once Jellyfin is up and running

The hard part is learning the ins and outs of your own server

With a Jellyfin server, once the libraries are configured, metadata is sorted, transcoding is working, and remote access is taken care of, the server largely disappears into the background. Mine has reached the point where I rarely think about it at all. Oh, and it doesn't sip $6.99 every month from my bank account.

Plex still has an advantage when other people are involved, though. I can hand a Plex account to someone who has never heard the words "Direct Play" or "hardware transcoding," and they can generally figure it out themselves. Jellyfin can offer a similarly polished experience, but getting someone there may require a small amount of tech support.

And that, more than any missing feature, is why Plex remains so difficult to displace. Jellyfin can become an exceptional media platform once you've built it properly, but Plex's greatest trick is making the person using your server completely unaware that there is a server behind it.
